question: A patient has psoriatic plaques covering approximately 15% of body surface area and a DLQI score of 12, with no pustular or erythrodermic features. Which treatment tier is most appropriate?

answers.text: Topical therapy alone, as the disease is mild

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. A BSA of 15% places the disease in the moderate range (10–20%), and a DLQI of 12 indicates significant quality-of-life impairment (≥10). Topical therapy alone is usually insufficient at this extent and impact level.

answers.text: Narrowband UVB phototherapy, with consideration of systemic agents if needed, as this is moderate disease with significant quality-of-life impairment

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. BSA of 10–20% defines moderate psoriasis, and DLQI ≥10 indicates significant impairment. Together these place the patient in the moderate tier, for which narrowband UVB phototherapy is appropriate, with escalation to systemic agents if the response is inadequate.
Incorrect. Systemic corticosteroids are contraindicated in psoriasis because their withdrawal can precipitate a rebound pustular or erythrodermic flare — regardless of disease severity.

answers.text: No treatment is needed below 20% body surface area

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Treatment decisions depend on BSA, PASI, and DLQI together. A DLQI of 12 alone warrants active treatment, and 15% BSA is moderate disease, not mild or negligible.

overallFeedback.feedback: BSA of 10–20% = moderate psoriasis; DLQI ≥10 = significant impairment. Together these indicate phototherapy (narrowband UVB) with systemic agents held in reserve. Systemic corticosteroids are always contraindicated in psoriasis.
Well done. Severity stratification uses BSA, PASI, and DLQI together — moderate disease (BSA 10–20% or DLQI ≥10) warrants phototherapy as first-line, not topicals alone.
